details:
**Sukkah (booths)**
The temporary hut that gives Sukkot its English names, the "Festival of Booths" or "Feast of Tabernacles." Observant Jews eat, and often sleep, in the sukkah throughout the holiday. It is traditionally built with at least three walls.

**Four Species**
The four plants held and waved together on Sukkot: the etrog (citron), the lulav (a palm frond), hadassim (myrtle branches), and aravot (willow branches). The palm, myrtle, and willow are bound together into a bundle that is also called the lulav.

**Etrog and lulav**
The two best-known items among the Four Species. The etrog is a lemon-like citron fruit, and the lulav is a closed date-palm frond bound together with the myrtle and willow. Worshippers hold them together during blessings and prayers.

**Na'anuim (shaking the Four Species)**
The ritual waving of the Four Species in six directions: the four directions of the compass, then up and down. It symbolizes God's presence everywhere.

**Ushpizin**
Aramaic for "guests"; the seven "exalted guests" ceremonially invited into the sukkah, one on each night of the festival. They are traditionally Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Joseph, and David.

**S'chach**
The roof covering of the sukkah, made of cut plant material such as palm leaves, branches, or bamboo. It must give more shade than sun, yet be sparse enough to see the stars through it.

**Wandering in the desert**
Sukkot began as a harvest festival (the "Feast of Ingathering") and was reinterpreted to commemorate the Israelites' forty years of wandering in the wilderness after the Exodus, when they lived in temporary shelters. Some traditions say the sukkah also recalls the protective "Clouds of Glory," sometimes represented by white sheets.

**15th of Tishrei**
The start date of Sukkot in the Hebrew calendar, five days after Yom Kippur. It is one of the three pilgrimage festivals, when Jews traditionally went up to the Temple in Jerusalem.

**Hoshana Rabbah**
"The Great Supplication," the seventh day of Sukkot. Worshippers circle the synagogue seven times reciting the hoshanot prayers (whose refrain is "Hosha na," "save us") and beat willow branches on the ground.

**Shemini Atzeret**
The "Eighth Day of Assembly," the holiday immediately following Sukkot. On it the Geshem prayer for rain is first recited. In many communities it is combined with or followed by Simchat Torah.

**Hakhel**
A biblical ceremony held on Sukkot once every seven years, after the sabbatical year. The king publicly read from the Torah (Deuteronomy) to the assembled people at the Temple.

**Samaritan pilgrimage to Mount Gerizim**
The Samaritans celebrate Sukkot as one of their three annual pilgrimage festivals to their holy mountain, Mount Gerizim. Because it falls in the autumn, it is the last of these pilgrimages in the calendar year.
